subject: chemistry
question_text: Explain the hybridization involved in the PCl₅ molecule.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book lists the bond angles as 90°, 180° and 120°; the card states 120° (equatorial) and 90° (axial-equatorial), with 180° recorded as the axial-axial angle.

steps.label: sp³d hybridisation of P
lines: In PCl₅ the central atom P undergoes sp³d
One 3s, three 3p and one 3d orbital mix to
give five identical sp³d hybrid orbitals.
steps.why: Phosphorus has only three unpaired electrons in the ground state, but PCl₅ needs five bonds. Excitation of one 3s electron into 3d gives five half-filled orbitals, which then mix into five sp³d hybrids.
common_mistakes: Writing sp³d² instead of sp³d. Five bonds need five hybrid orbitals, so only ONE d orbital joins.
Skipping the excited state line. The excitation is what creates the five unpaired electrons.
steps.memory_tip: Count the bonds first: five bonds means five hybrids, so s + three p + one d.
steps.margin_note: Write the excited state configuration before naming the hybrids.

steps.label: Overlap with chlorine
lines: Each half-filled sp³d hybrid orbital of P
steps.why: The bond count follows from the overlap: five hybrids on P, one half-filled 3p orbital on each Cl, so five axial overlaps and five σ bonds.
common_mistakes: Calling the P–Cl bonds π bonds. Axial overlap gives σ bonds.
Leaving out chlorine's configuration, which shows WHY each Cl brings exactly one half-filled orbital.
steps.memory_tip: Each Cl brings one half-filled 3p orbital; each P hybrid meets one of them.
steps.margin_note: Name the bond type in full: σ(sp³d–p).

steps.label: The diagram
steps.why: The shape mark needs the drawn arrangement: two axial bonds on the vertical line and three equatorial bonds in the middle plane. The dashed bond shows one equatorial Cl behind the plane of the page.
common_mistakes: Drawing all five Cl atoms at equal angles around P. Two are axial and three are equatorial, and they are not equivalent.
Leaving the angle labels off. The 90° and 120° labels carry part of the mark.
steps.memory_tip: Draw the vertical axis first (two Cl), then the triangle around the middle (three Cl).
steps.margin_note: A neat small diagram is enough. Label at least one 90° and one 120° angle.

steps.label: Shape and bond angles

lines.text: Shape: trigonal bipyramidal — bond angles 120° and 90°

lines: Three equatorial bonds lie in one plane at
120° to each other; the two axial bonds
steps.why: Naming the shape and giving the two distinct bond angles shows the geometry is understood, not just the hybrid count.
common_mistakes: Writing a single bond angle. Trigonal bipyramidal has two different angles, 120° and 90°.
Calling the shape triangular bipyramidal or pentagonal. The name is trigonal bipyramidal.
steps.memory_tip: Five positions split as 3 + 2: three in the triangle (120°), two on the axis (90° to it).
steps.margin_note: Shape name plus both angles closes the answer.

insider_note: Write the excited state configuration before naming the five hybrid orbitals — that line is where this question's method mark sits.
